list.listitem: Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 2 is an autosomal dominant neoplasia syndrome dominated by medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) with high penetrance. It has several variants including familial medullary thyroid cancer (FMTC), MEN 2a, and MEN 2b.
Screening for these mutations and implementation of prophylactic thyroidectomy for those who are positive is of paramount importance in improving the outcome. B
All of these variants are secondary to activating germline mutations in RET oncogene.

Measurements of serum calcitonin, 24-hour urine catacholamines and/or metanephrines, and serum calcium and parathyroid hormone are excellent methods for diagnosis and monitoring of MTC, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT), respectively. B
Surgery is the primary modality of treatment for all tumors of MEN 2 syndromes, with prophylactic thyroidectomy recommended in children at a young age. A

background.definition: The term multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) refers to a pair of autosomal dominant familial neoplasia syndromes, MEN 1 and MEN 2. MEN 2 is further subclassified into familial medullary thyroid cancer (FMTC), MEN 2a, and MEN 2b (). To avoid mislabeling of MEN 2a as FMTC with the risk of missing pheochromocytoma, the diagnosis of FMTC requires multiple carriers in the kindred with multiple carriers above the age of 50 years and adequate medical history especially in older carriers.

list.listitem: MEN 2 syndromes are autosomal dominant disorders with very high penetrance.
All subtypes of MEN 2 and familial medullary thyroid cancer (FMTC) are caused by germline mutations in the RET oncogene.
RET encodes a plasma membrane-spanning tyrosine kinase receptor.
In MEN 2 and FMTC, RET mutations lead to constitutive activation of the receptor kinase activity causing oncogenic and transforming changes.
Constitutively activating mutations in RET cause chronic ligand-independent activation of the receptor.
This chronic overstimulation of RET tyrosine kinase activity leads to activation of downstream intracellular effectors with consequent cellular transformation.
There is a very good genotype-phenotype correlation.
Screening for RET oncogene mutations is highly accurate and effective. A
Those with positive RET mutations should undergo evaluation for the presence of MTC, pheochromocytoma, and PHPT. A

If there is no evidence of disease, prophylactic total thyroidectomy is recommended before the age of 5 years for those with FMTC or MEN 2a and before the age of 6 months for MEN 2b. Surgery should be avoided in high risk children (as defined by American Thyroid Association guidelines) before the age of 3 years.B

Following prophylactic thyroidectomy, long-term follow-up and periodic screening for pheochromocytoma using daily urinary excretion of catacholamines or its metabolites or serum metanephrines and for primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) in MEN 2a using serum calcium are recommended. B
Elevated, random calcium- or pentagastrin-stimulated serum calcitonin (3-fold above upper normal limit) suggests MTC. B
Measurements of urinary excretion of catecholamines or metanephrines in a 24-hour urine sample or serum metanephrines are used for diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. B

For pheochromocytoma, computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and/or metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan are used for localization of primary tumor and screening for metastases or multiple tumors. B
Elevated serum calcium in the presence of elevated or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone is consistent with the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT). B
Localizing procedures are not usually needed in PHPT because surgery entails all-gland exploration. B

Medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) is usually the first and dominant manifestation of all MEN 2 syndromes. If not diagnosed in the preclinical stage by genetic screening, patients with MTC usually present with asymptomatic thyroid nodule.

Patients with long-standing MTC may also develop cervical lymphadenopathy or local pressure symptoms such as pain, dysphagia, voice change, choking, cough, or difficulty in breathing. Patients with distant metastases may complain of chronic diarrhea and symptoms related to the site of metastases (eg, bone pain from skeletal metastasis).

Pheochromocytoma develops in around 50% of patients, usually in patients who had MTC or were known to have MEN 2 syndromes. At the onset, it may be asymptomatic because the secretion of catecholamines is usually mild but when symptomatic, patients may present with the classic triad of palpitations, sweating and headaches, anxiety, weight loss, constipation, or psychiatric symptoms.

Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) in MEN 2a develops in about 20% to 30% of cases, usually at a later stage and is frequently asymptomatic when discovered on screening by the finding of hypercalcemia. When symptomatic, it is not different from sporadic PHPT presenting with neuromuscular, neuropsychiatric, gastrointestinal symptoms, and nephrolithiasis.

For medullary thyroid cancer (MTC), random serum calcitonin and calcium- or pentagastrin-stimulated calcitonin may indicate an early MTC even before it is visible on high-resolution neck ultrasonography. Calcium-stimulation test is performed by giving calcium gluconate 2.5 mg/kg intravenously (IV) over 30 seconds and measuring calcitonin at baseline, 2, and 5 minutes. Pentagastrin-stimulated calcitonin is measured serially at 0, 2, 3.5, and 5 minutes after rapid IV injection of pentagastrin 0.5 mg/kg given over 10 seconds; an increment in calcitonin of more than 3-folds in either test is considered positive. Combination of these tests might be more accurate.

A study identified a basal serum calcitonin level >19.0 pmol/L as an optimal cutoff for detection of MTC (77% sensitive, 97% specific). However, approximately 1 in 4 patiens with MTC have a level below this cutoff.
US practice guidelines recommend a calcitonin cutoff of 150 pg/ml for prompting further evaluation for metastatic disease in patients undergoing surveillance after treatment.
If neck ultrasonography reveals a nodule, fine needle aspiration biopsy is indicated.
See chapters on hyperparathyroidism and pheochromocytoma for detailed discussion of diagnosis of those conditions.

Localization techniques are usually not needed for PHPT because the surgery in MEN 2 entails 4-gland exploration, ultrasonography, and 99m-technetium sestamibi scans are sometimes used for this purpose.
Patients diagnosed with MTC should be evaluated for the RET mutation, and if positive undergo evaluation for hyperparathyroidism and pheochromocytoma.
When there is a family history of MEN 2 or FMTC, screening for RET mutations is the most cost-effective initial step.

If a RET mutation in a family with MEN 2 or FMTC is known, limited screening focusing on the same mutation is recommended. When the mutation is unknown, screening RET oncogene for all known mutations is necessary.
For those with a positive mutation, evaluation for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism should occur.

For medullary thyroid cancer (MTC): Total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection is recommended for all cases of MTC. Lateral neck dissection is recommended for those with suspicious lymph nodes on preoperative imaging studies or during intraoperative examination. The tyrosine kinase inhibitors vandetanib and cabozantinib are options for patients with unresecta ble disease.B

For pheochromocytoma: After proper preoperative preparation, which includes alpha with or without beta adrenergic receptor blockers and generous volume expansion, unilateral or bilateral adrenalectomy is recommended for unilateral or bilateral pheochromocytoma, respectively. This is usually done laproscopically. B
MIBG therapy might be of benefit for patients with residual or metastatic pheochromocytoma. C
For primary hyperparathyroidism, subtotal parathyroidectomy (3½ gland removal) with or without autotransplantation is recommended. B

Medullary thyroid cancer (MTC): Surgery is the only definitive therapy for MTC (see below). The tyrosine kinase inhibitors vandetanib and cabozantinib have both been approved for treatment of medullary thyroid cancers. They have been shown in RCTs of patients with unresectble locally advanced or metastatic MTC to lead to improved median progression free survival. Somatostatin analogs are effective for control of diarrhea in cases of metastatic or inoperable disease, for example, long-acting octreotide 20 to 40 mg intramuscularly once in 28 days.

Pheochromocytoma: Surgery is also the definitive therapy for pheochromocytoma. Alpha adrenergic receptor blockers such as phenoxybenzamine 10 to 20 mg twice a day (bid) with or without beta adrenergic receptor blockers (eg, propranolol 20-40 mg once in 6 hours) or combined alpha and beta blockers (labetalol 100-200 mg bid) are important drugs for preoperative preparation and for symptomatic control in cases of functionally active inoperable or metastatic tumor.
Primary hyperparathyroidism: Surgery is the only effective mode of therapy for symptomatic PHPT. In cases of asymptomatic mild PHPT, expectant follow-up may suffice.

For patients with positive RET mutation screen and no clinical evidence of MTC, prophylactic total thyroidectomy with or without central compartment neck clearance is indicated before the age of 5 years for mutations associated with FMTC and MEN 2a, and before the age of 6 months for mutations associated with MEN 2b.

For clinically or radiologically apparent MTC or when the random or stimulated calcitonin are elevated, total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection is the surgery of choice. Lateral neck dissection is indicated if there is evidence of lymph node involvement either on preoperative evaluation or during intraoperative examination.
Subtotal parathyroidectomy (3½ gland removal) and parathyroid tissue autotransplantation is recommended as surgery for primary hyperparathyroidism.
With the wide availability of laparoscopic surgery, unilateral adrenalectomy is recommended for unilateral pheochromocytoma. Bilateral adrenalectomy is indicated for bilateral disease.
For patients with medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) that is locally invasive and not completely removed at surgery, external beam radiotherapy may have an adjunctive role.
For metastatic or incompletely resectable pheochromocytoma, metaiodobenzylguanidine therapy and systemic chemotherapy may provide some benefit.
Other therapies of limited effectiveness for metastatic MTC or pheochromocytoma include interferon-alpha alone or in combination with somatostatin analogs and immunotherapy.
Recently, angiogenesis inhibitors including tyrosine kinase inhibitors that target RET and vascular endothelial growth factor receptor showed some promising results in MTC.
MEN 2 syndromes have variable prognosis. Medullary thyroid cancer is the usual cause of death. B
Early detection and treatment are the most important prognostic factors. B
Prognosis is best in FMTC, followed by MEN 2a and MEN 2b. B
About 40% of persons with MEN 2 develop pheochromocytoma.

Medullary thyroid cancer: Random and stimulated serum calcitonin is used for monitoring for recurrence after thyroidectomy. Carcinoembryonic antigen is also useful especially if it was elevated before surgery. US practice guidelines recommend physical examination and ultrasound of the neck, plus measuresment of serum calcitonin, carcinoembryonic antigen, and thyroid function tests every 6 to 12 months.

Different imaging techniques are used for monitoring of local recurrence or distant metastasis. Neck ultrasonography is an excellent tool for neck recurrence and CT, MRI, and other techniques for distant metastases.
For pheochromocytoma: 24-hour urinary excretion of catacholamines or metanephrines is used. MIBG scans and other imaging techniques are used for localization of sites of recurrence.
Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone are used for detection of recurrence of primary hyperparathyoidism.
